transcript: Senator from Utah, Mr. Hatch. Now, Mr. President, during the 101st Congress, I was pleased to work with the distinguished senator from Ohio on the nutritional labeling and education act. And I was, and I am proud of our work together. This is a very, very important bill. And I still believe that it is a fundamentally good piece of legislation, and I hope to support its full and complete implementation very soon. But Mr. President, we have discovered that this law was not perfect. We made a mistake, hard for any of us to admit. I know, but we did. We should have spelled out our intent even more specifically, so the FDA would have no question about it. We should have been clear that we did not intend the FDA to treat dietary supplements like drugs. which is the way they're trading, or they intend to treat them. But instead, we left it up to the FDA to determine categories for regulation of health claims. And unfortunately, the FDA decided to put herbs in the same regulatory category as tetracycline and vitamin A in the same category as insulin. Now, the people in this country outraged by this, and I am too. Today, we can take the first step in correcting this mistake. We can prevent FDA from implementing these regulations for an additional year. We can prevent the FDA from denying the health claims of many tried and true dietary supplements. The FDA is an agency for which I have a great deal of respect, and as my colleagues know, Mr. President, I help to lead the fight in the Senate for the FDA revitalization bill. It's a Hatch bill. It's commissioner, Dr. David Kessler, is a former substantial member of my staff. I have a great deal of love and affection for him. I believe that he's a wonderful commissioner in most every way. And I have helped to promote and support the FDA as the nation's consumer watchdog, have stood up for it in every case. But I'm burned up at the way they are drafting these regulations and the indications that they're going to treat food supplements and vitamins and minerals and herbal preparations and other natural substances like drugs. I think the agency is over-reaching this particular case. This situation is a clear-cut example of over-regulation. Mr. President, the FDA is at the forefront of protecting consumers from unsafe foods and drugs, and it has been effective and will be. And I'll support it. It deservedly receives kudos from Congress, the President, and the people. But let me say that if the Congress of the United States is not perfect, neither is the FDA. In this case, it is patently wrong. There is no case to be made for such strict regulation of health claims for dietary supplements. And admitting mistakes is not criminal. Most Americans have made them from time to time, and generally, they are understanding when we act to correct our mistakes. Americans admire intellectual honesty. What burns them up is when Congress refuses to own up to the obvious, such as when we resisted fixing the catastrophic health care bill, or Section 89. Has anyone in this body forgotten the hue and cry from our constituents on those issues? Well, if you think that was bad, what do you see what happens if we allow the FDA to continue its over-regulatory, heavy-handed approach towards vitamins, minerals, food supplements, and herbal preparations? Would any of us care to repeat the experiences on catastrophic health? Now, Mr. President, the amendment I am offering will not permanently solve the problem created by the Nutrition, Labeling, and Education Act. I have proposed legislation that ultimately will. What this amendment will do is delay implementation of the detrimental regulations. Read that mistakes. That's the way it should read of the Nutrition Labeling and Education Act for one year so that we can work out an acceptable long-term solution. Let me restate that all other components of the regulations will go into effect on schedule. This won't hurt them at all. Nor do I believe this will be taken out at conference. Because many of those on the other side of the Capitol agree with me that the FDA has been too heavy-handed and has been too over-regulatory in its approach to food supplements. Additionally, I want to reiterate that the FDA will continue to retain its existing authority to pull any product whatsoever off the market if it is toxic, deleterious, or poisonous, or otherwise injurious to people. They have that power, and this amendment will not take that away neither would my bill. But Mr. President, I would not be standing here today if I did not truly believe The FDA's position on this matter is in error. I would not be here today if there were convincing evidence that herbs, vitamins, amino acids, or other supplements were harmful to health. They are not. I would not be standing here if the FDA or the opponents of the amendment for that matter were open-minded on the subject of differentiating between everyday substances and pharmaceuticals when it comes to regulatory categories. How on earth can a health claim for bee pollen be in the same category as a health claim for an ulcer medication treatment? It is time for the FDA to infuse a little common sense into its role-making. And let's fix this mistake once and for all. Let's begin right here today with, I hope, an overwhelming vote by postponing the implementation of it and send a message to FDA that we are not going to tolerate this type of over-regulatory, heavy-handed, administrative approaches. If I seem worked up on this, I am. And I know that there are millions around this country even more worked out, as they see little health food stores rated by FDA inspectors. As they see doctors, FDA inspired people going in there with flak, vests, and guns. And taking away the doctor's equipment and the doctor's own properties. It's time to stop this type of thing and get some reason into it. And if we have reason, the American people will comply with the reason. What's involved here is the FDA has proposed regulations that would treat dietary supplements such as vitamins, minerals, herbal preparations and so forth as prescription drugs. for purposes of making health claims. If they succeed in that, I can't tell you the cost of vitamins and minerals will go off the charts. The average person won't be able to even afford. Now, the Hatch amendment would impose a simple one-year moratorium on this implementation of these regulations so that a comprehensive long-term solution can be found. And that's what we want to do here. But I would call all of my colleagues' attention to the Health Freedom Act of 1992 S2835. That's the legislation that will pass later. If we can't get FDA to wake up and realize that we're not going to put up with this type of heavy-headed over-regulatory methodology. This legislation, the Health Freedom Act of 1992, will help to ensure that companies producing dietary supplements can do so without unnecessary regulatory constraints. Mr. President, I ask unanimous consent that a dear colleague letter signed by me be placed in the record at this point. 20
